passages.title: Planting Bean Seeds
sentences: Ms. Ortiz gave each pair in her class a sheet of directions for planting bean seeds in the school garden.
Before you plant, check how wet the soil is in your garden bed.
Push one finger into the soil, all the way down to your second knuckle.
If the soil feels dry at that depth, pour one full watering can over the bed and wait ten minutes.
If it already feels damp, you can begin planting right away.
Next, use the inch marks on your trowel handle to make a straight row of holes.
Each hole should be about one inch deep, and the holes should be four inches apart.
Drop one bean seed into each hole, and then gently cover it with loose soil.
Do not press the soil down hard, because the young roots need air to grow.
Finally, push a craft-stick label into the end of your row.
Write both of your names and today's date on the label in pencil, since marker ink can wash off in the rain.
Water the row lightly, just until the top of the soil looks dark.
The first green shoots should appear in about seven to ten days.

passages.title: Calibrating the Rover's Distance Sensor
sentences: Priya's rover uses a distance sensor to stop before it bumps into a wall.
The sensor sends out a sound too high for people to hear, and then it measures how long the echo takes to bounce back.
Before each competition, the robotics club calibrates the sensor, which means checking that its readings match real, measured distances.
To begin, place the rover on a flat table with its sensor facing a cardboard box.
Use a ruler to measure exactly 20 centimeters from the front of the sensor to the box.
Next, connect the rover to the club laptop with the USB cable and open the program called SensorCheck.
Press the Read button three times, and write down each number that appears on the screen.
Now compare your three readings with the real distance of 20 centimeters.
If all three readings are between 19 and 21 centimeters, the sensor is accurate, and you can unplug the cable.
If the readings are all too high or all too low, type the difference into the Offset box and press Save.
For example, if the sensor reads 23 centimeters each time, the difference is 3, so you type minus 3.
Then press Read three more times to make sure your fix worked.
Sometimes the three numbers jump around instead, such as 15, 28 and 20.
Jumping numbers usually mean that the sensor is dusty or that the box is too small to send back a clear echo.
In that case, wipe the sensor gently with a dry cloth, move to a larger box, and start the whole test again from the beginning.

passages.title: Setting Up a Weather Station
sentences: Priya's family bought a SkyCheck weather station for their backyard.
It has two parts: an outdoor sensor and an indoor display.
The sensor measures the temperature and the humidity outside, and it sends the numbers to the display by radio.
Humidity means how much water vapor is in the air.
First, put two AA batteries into the outdoor sensor.
Within one minute, put three AAA batteries into the display, so the display can connect to the sensor.
Keep both parts on the same table while they connect.
After about three minutes, the outdoor temperature should appear on the screen.
If you still see two dashes instead of a number, take the batteries out of the display, wait ten seconds, and put them back in.
Next, choose a home for the sensor.
Hang it on a post about five feet above the ground, in a spot that is shady all day, such as under a tree.
Sunlight shining on the sensor makes it read warmer than the air really is.
Keep it away from walls, roofs and driveways too, because they soak up the sun's heat and give it off later.
Last, set the display indoors, no more than 100 feet from the sensor.

passages.title: Tide Pool Checklist
sentences: Ms. Ortiz is taking the science club to the tide pools at Harbor Point on Saturday.
A tide pool is a shallow pocket of seawater that remains trapped among the rocks after the tide goes out.
Sea stars, hermit crabs, periwinkle snails and sea anemones all live in these pools.
Before the trip, Ms. Ortiz sent every club member this checklist.
First, check the tide table, because you can reach the pools only when the tide is low.
On Saturday, low tide at Harbor Point is at 10:40 AM.
Plan to reach the rocks about one hour before low tide.
Start walking back to the sand no later than one hour after low tide, because the water keeps rising and covers the low rocks.
If you lose track of the time, listen for Ms. Ortiz, who will blow her whistle three times when it is time to go back.
Next, pack your bag the night before.
Wear old sneakers or water shoes with sturdy rubber soles, because wet seaweed makes the rocks extremely slippery.
Bring a hat, a water bottle, and a notebook and pencil for your field notes.
Leave buckets and nets at home, because every creature must remain in its own pool.
At the pools, observe carefully before you touch anything.
If you want to touch an animal, wet your hand in the pool first and use only one finger, very gently.
Never pull an animal off a rock, because many of them attach themselves firmly to the rock, and pulling can injure them.
If you lift a small rock to look underneath, put it back exactly the way it was, because animals live on its underside.

passages.title: Tuning a Guitar
sentences: Sam is learning to play the guitar in the Harbor Middle School music club.
Before every practice, he tunes his guitar, which means making each string play exactly the right note.
A guitar has six strings, and in standard tuning they are E, A, D, G, B and E, from the thickest string to the thinnest.
The club leader gave Sam these steps for using a clip-on tuner.
First, clip the tuner onto the head of the guitar, where the tuning pegs are, and switch it on.
Next, pluck the thickest string once and let it ring.
The tuner shows the letter of the note it hears, along with a needle.
If the needle points left of the center, the note is flat, or too low, so slowly turn that string's peg to tighten the string.
If the needle points right of the center, the note is sharp, or too high, so loosen the string a little.
When the needle stays in the center and the screen turns green, that string is in tune.
Strings stay in tune longer when you finish by tightening, so if you go past the note, loosen the string below it and then tighten it back up.
Repeat these steps for each of the other five strings, from thickest to thinnest.
Sometimes the tuner shows the wrong letter, such as G when you are tuning the A string.
In music, G is the note just below A, so that string is much too low, and you should keep tightening it slowly until the letter changes to A.
Always turn the pegs slowly, because a string that is pulled much too tight can snap.
When all six strings are in tune, check each one again, because tuning one string pulls a little on the others.

passages.title: Two-Day Pizza Dough
sentences: Grandma Rose is teaching Sam to make pizza dough for Saturday's family pizza night.
Her dough takes two days, because it rests in the refrigerator overnight, which gives it more flavor.
On Friday evening, stir 3 cups of flour, 1 teaspoon of salt and 1 teaspoon of yeast together in a large bowl.
Pour in 1 cup of warm water and stir until a rough, lumpy dough forms.
Knead the dough on a floured counter for 8 minutes, until it feels smooth and stretchy.
If the dough sticks to your hands, sprinkle on a spoonful of flour, but add no more than 3 spoonfuls in all.
Too much flour makes the crust dry and tough.
Put the dough in an oiled bowl, cover it, and place it in the refrigerator.
On Saturday, take the dough out of the refrigerator two hours before you plan to bake.
Cold dough is stiff, and it springs back when you try to stretch it.
Ask an adult to heat the oven to 475°F for 30 minutes before baking.
Press the dough into a circle with your fingertips, and if it shrinks back, let it rest for 10 minutes before you try again.

passages.title: The Floating Egg
sentences: Ms. Ortiz's science club is testing why people float more easily in the ocean than in a lake.
Ocean water has salt dissolved in it.
The salt makes the water denser, which means a cup of it is heavier than a cup of fresh water.
Denser water pushes up harder on things, so they float higher.
Each pair of students needs two tall clear glasses, warm tap water, a spoon, table salt and two raw eggs.
Fill both glasses halfway with warm water, and label one glass FRESH and the other SALT.
Stir 6 spoonfuls of salt into the SALT glass, one spoonful at a time, until you can no longer see the grains.
Then use the spoon to lower one egg gently into each glass.
Write down what each egg does: it may sink to the bottom, float in the middle, or float at the top.
If the egg in the SALT glass still sinks, lift it out, stir in 2 more spoonfuls of salt, and test again.
Keep adding salt this way until the egg floats.
If grains of salt stay on the bottom no matter how long you stir, the water cannot hold any more salt.
In that case, record what happened and stop adding salt.
Last, pour the salt water down the sink with plenty of tap water.
Wash your hands with soap, because raw eggs can carry germs.

passages.title: How to Map a Creek
sentences: Mr. Lee's class is making a map of a short part of the creek in Story Woods.
Each group of three has a measuring tape, a compass, a clipboard and a sheet of grid paper.
Their map uses a scale, which tells how a distance on the paper matches a distance on the ground.
On this map, one grid square across equals 2 meters on the ground.
First, choose a starting point, such as the big flat rock, and mark it with a dot near the bottom left corner of the paper.
Next, one person holds the compass flat and finds north.
Draw a small arrow pointing to the top of the page, and label it N.
Then two people stretch the tape from the starting point to the next landmark, such as the footbridge.
Divide the distance in meters by 2 to find how many squares to draw.
For example, 10 meters becomes 5 squares on the paper.
Repeat the measuring for each landmark, and draw a symbol for it.
If a landmark is in the water, such as a fallen log, do not wade into the creek to measure it.
Instead, estimate the distance from the bank, and write the word about next to that distance on your map.
When you finish, add a key that explains each symbol.

passages.title: Casting a Dinosaur Footprint
sentences: At the Harbor Town Museum, Dr. Bell is leading a workshop on casting dinosaur footprints.
A cast is a copy made by pouring a liquid into a shape and letting it harden.
The museum has rubber molds of real footprints left by a three-toed dinosaur.
First, brush a thin layer of cooking oil inside the mold, so the plaster will not stick to it.
Then mix 2 cups of plaster powder with 1 cup of cool water, and stir slowly for one minute, until it is as thick as pancake batter.
Pour the plaster into the mold, and tap the sides gently so air bubbles rise to the top.
As the plaster hardens, it will feel warm, which is normal.
Leave it alone for 30 minutes.
After 30 minutes, press the edge with one fingernail.
If your nail leaves a dent, wait 15 more minutes and test again.
When the plaster feels hard and cool, bend the rubber mold back and lift out your cast.
Let the cast dry overnight before you paint it, because paint does not stick well to damp plaster.
The next day, paint the footprint, and write your name and the date on the back.

sentences: Ana and Ben are running a Comet Karts video game tournament at the Harbor Town Library on Saturday.
Eight players signed up, and Mrs. Hall set up three screens in the meeting room: two for matches and one for free play.
Ben wrote the rules on the whiteboard so everyone could follow them.
Each match is between two players and has up to three races.
The first player to win two races wins the match, so if one player wins the first two races, the third race is skipped.
The winner moves on to the next round, and the other player may use the free-play screen.
Matches 1 and 2 happen at the same time, one on each match screen.
Matches 3 and 4 start together when both match screens are free.
If two karts cross the finish line in a tie, those two players race that track again.

passages.title: Building a Bird Feeder
sentences: Sam and Grandma Rose are building a wooden bird feeder from a kit.
The kit comes with a tray, a roof, four short posts, eight screws and a metal hook.
First, screw the four posts into the corners of the tray.
Set the roof on top of the posts and screw it in place.
Then twist the metal hook into the center of the roof.
Hang the feeder from a branch at least 5 feet above the ground, so cats cannot reach the birds while they eat.
Choose a spot near bushes or trees, where small birds can hide quickly.
Fill the tray with black sunflower seeds, which many kinds of birds like to eat.
Birds may take a week or more to find a new feeder, so leave it in the same place even if none come right away.
Check the feeder every two days, and add seeds when the tray is less than half full.
If the seeds get wet and clump together, throw them away and wipe the tray dry, because wet seeds can grow mold that makes birds sick.
Every two weeks, take the feeder down, scrub it with warm soapy water, rinse it, and let it dry completely before you refill it.
If squirrels keep eating the seeds, ask an adult to add a squirrel guard, which is a wide cone that hangs above the feeder.

Both jobs can happen at the same time, but everything must be ready by 6:15 PM, when the band starts to tune.
Leo starts with the bass drum, the biggest drum, which stands on its side on the floor.
He clips the bass drum pedal to the front of it, where his right foot can reach it.
Next, he sets the drum stool at a height where his knees are a little lower than his hips.
The snare drum goes on its stand between his knees.
The hi-hat cymbals go on his left side, with their pedal under his left foot.
Last, he places the two small tom drums above the bass drum.
He sets the large cymbal where he can reach it easily.
Meanwhile, Sam and Maya set up twenty chairs in four rows of five, all facing Ms. Gray's stand.

If a stand wobbles, they tighten the knob on its pole, or they swap it for a spare from the closet.

Each team plays three games, and each game lasts 40 minutes.

Our first game starts at 9:00 AM on Field 2.
Our second game is at 11:00 AM on Field 4, and our third game is at 1:00 PM on Field 2.
After you check in, we will warm up together.
First, jog two laps around the field, then stretch for five minutes, and then practice passing in pairs.
Between games, sit in the shade, drink water, and eat the snack you packed.
If anyone hears thunder or sees lightning, the referees will stop all games right away.
Walk calmly with the team to the school gym next to the fields, and wait inside with me.
Games can start again only after 30 minutes pass with no thunder.

passages.title: Starting a Sourdough Starter
sentences: A sourdough starter is a mix of flour and water that collects wild yeast from the flour and from the air around it.
As the yeast feeds on the flour, it makes tiny bubbles of gas, and those bubbles later help bread rise.
Grandma Rose is teaching a sourdough class at Rose's Bakery, and Maya and Priya are taking it.
She gave each student a glass jar and a schedule.
A new starter takes about a week to become strong enough for baking.
On Day 1, stir together 1/2 cup of whole wheat flour and 1/2 cup of lukewarm water in the clean jar.
Scrape down the sides, put a rubber band around the jar at the top of the mix, and cover the jar loosely with a cloth.
Keep the jar on the counter, out of direct sunlight.
For the next five days, feed the starter once a day at about the same time.
To feed it, pour out half of the starter, then stir in 1/2 cup of flour and 1/4 cup of water.
Pouring out half may seem wasteful, but if you skip it, the jar will overflow, and the yeast will run out of food.
Each time you feed it, move the rubber band to the new top of the mix.
On some days, you may see a layer of gray liquid on top.
This liquid means the starter is hungry, so pour it off and feed the starter right away, even if it is not feeding time yet.
If you see pink or orange streaks or fuzzy spots, harmful mold is growing.
In that case, throw the whole starter away and begin again in a clean jar.
Your starter is ready when it doubles in height within 6 hours of a feeding, rising to twice as high as the rubber band.

passages.title: How to Pan for Gold
sentences: At the Ridgeway Mine Museum, Mr. Varga teaches visitors how miners once panned for gold in mountain streams.
Gold is much heavier than sand or gravel of the same size, so when a pan of wet gravel is shaken, the gold sinks to the bottom.
The goal of panning is to wash the light material away while the heavy material stays behind.
First, fill your pan about three-quarters full of gravel from the bucket.
Hold the pan under the water in the long trough, and rub the gravel with your fingers to break up any clumps of mud.
Pick out the large stones, but look at each one for gold before you toss it aside.
Next, keep the pan under the water and shake it hard from side to side for about thirty seconds.
The shaking lets the heavy pieces settle to the bottom.
Now lift the pan until its rim is just below the surface, and tilt it slightly away from you.
Swirl it in small circles so the water carries the top layer of light gravel over the far edge.
Repeat the shaking and the swirling, again and again, until only about a spoonful of dark, heavy sand remains.
If you tilt the pan too steeply, you may wash the gold away too, so keep the tilt gentle.
Finally, add a little clean water and swirl it slowly to spread out the dark sand.
Gold shows up as tiny bright yellow flecks that stay in place when you move the pan.
If you see shiny gold-colored flakes that float or wash away easily, they are probably mica, a light mineral that only looks like gold.
Use the plastic tweezers to put your gold flecks in a small tube of water, and Mr. Varga will label it with your name.

passages.title: Using the Club Telescope
sentences: Dr. Lee is lending the astronomy club a small telescope from the Lantern Peaks Observatory for a night of stargazing.
Before she hands it over, she goes through her setup steps with Priya and Sam.
The most important rule comes first: never point the telescope at the Sun, not even for a second.
The Sun's strong light, focused by the telescope, can harm your eyes.
Set up the tripod on flat, solid ground, and spread its legs wide so it stays steady.
Attach the telescope, and then line up the small finder scope on its side while it is still light outside.
To do this, aim the main telescope at a distant treetop.
Then turn the finder's two screws until the same treetop sits in the center of its crosshairs.
Lining up the finder in daylight is much easier than doing it in the dark.
At night, always start with the eyepiece that has the larger number on it, which is 25 mm.
A larger number means lower magnification, so you see a wider part of the sky, and finding an object is easier.
Once the object is in the center of the view, you can switch to the 10 mm eyepiece to see it larger.
If the view looks blurry, turn the focus knob slowly in one direction, and if it gets worse, turn it back the other way.
Stars and planets slowly drift out of view, because Earth is turning.
When an object reaches the edge of the view, nudge the telescope gently to bring it back to the center.
When you finish, put the caps back on both ends before you fold up the tripod, so dust cannot get inside.

passages.title: Jacketing a Fossil
sentences: Dr. Bell is showing the museum's young volunteers how her team protects a large fossil before moving it.
A fossil bone that has been underground for millions of years is often cracked.
It can fall apart if someone simply lifts it out of the ground.
So paleontologists wrap it in a hard shell called a plaster jacket.
First, dig a trench around the bone, leaving the bone sitting on a column of rock and dirt called a pedestal.
Make the trench deep enough that you can reach under the pedestal later.
Next, cover every exposed part of the bone with damp paper towels.
This layer keeps the plaster from sticking to the fossil, so the jacket can be removed later in the lab.
Then dip strips of burlap cloth into a bucket of wet plaster, squeeze off the extra, and lay them over the paper towels.
Overlap the strips by about half their width, and smooth each one with your hands so there are no gaps or air pockets.
Add at least two layers, and wrap the strips partway down the sides of the pedestal.
If the plaster in the bucket starts to thicken before you finish, mix a fresh batch instead of adding water to the old one.
Let the jacket harden for at least one hour, or overnight if the air is cool and damp.
Once it is hard, carefully dig under the pedestal until the jacket breaks free.
Then flip it over with help from two or three people.
Finally, plaster the open bottom the same way, and write the date and a number on the jacket so the team can match it to their field map.

passages.title: The Line-Following Rover
sentences: In the next robotics contest, Priya's rover must follow a black line taped on a white floor, from the start box to the finish box.
Two light sensors sit under the front of the rover, one on each side of the line.
A white floor reflects a lot of light back to a sensor, while black tape reflects very little.
Priya's program follows three rules.
If both sensors see white, the line is between them, so the rover drives straight ahead.
If the left sensor sees black, the rover has drifted to the right, so it turns left until that sensor sees white again.
If the right sensor sees black, the rover turns right in the same way.
Before each test run, Priya sets the speed to 40 and the turn strength to 5.
Then she places the rover in the start box with the line centered under it.
During the run, a teammate times it with a stopwatch and writes down anything that goes wrong.
The rules allow three test runs before the real contest run.
Priya also made a short list of fixes for common problems.
If the rover wobbles from side to side on straight parts, lower the turn strength by 1.
If it shoots off the line at sharp curves, lower the speed by 10, because the sensors cannot react fast enough at high speed.
If it stops in the middle of the course, check that the battery is above 50 percent before you change any numbers.
Change only one number between runs, so you can tell which change made the difference.

passages.title: Taking Your Bike on the Ferry
sentences: On Saturday, Sam and his dad are taking their bikes to Gull Island on the Harbor Town ferry.
Captain Ruth Lane's ferry has a special deck for bikes, but it holds only twelve, so riders with bikes follow some extra steps.
The ferry leaves the harbor at 9:00 AM, and the crossing takes 40 minutes.
First, buy your tickets at the ticket window.
A rider ticket costs $5, and each bike needs its own $3 bike ticket.
The window opens at 8:30 AM, and the twelve bike tickets often sell out on sunny weekends.
Next, wait with your bike in Lane B, the lane painted with green stripes.
Riders with bikes board first, starting 25 minutes before the ferry leaves, and cars board after them.
Boarding closes 10 minutes before the ferry leaves, and the crew cannot open the gate again after that.
Walk your bike up the ramp, and never ride it, because the metal ramp is slippery when it is wet.
On the lower deck, a crew member will show you which rack to use.
Hook your front wheel into the rack and wrap the strap around the frame.
Then carry your helmet, water bottle and anything else you need up to the passenger deck, because no one may stay on the bike deck during the crossing.
When the ferry docks, wait until a crew member calls the bike riders down to the lower deck.
If the bike tickets are sold out, you can lock your bike at the racks beside the ticket window and ride the ferry without it.

passages.title: Weather Journal Week
sentences: Ms. Ortiz's class is keeping a weather journal for five school days, from Monday to Friday.
Every student records the same measurements at exactly the same time, 12:00 noon, so the class can compare observations at the end of the week.
The tools are kept in the white weather box outside the science room, next to a tall pole with a wind vane on top.
First, read the thermometer in the shade, and record the temperature in degrees Fahrenheit.
Next, look up at the sky and name the main type of cloud.
Puffy white clouds with flat bottoms are cumulus clouds.
A flat gray sheet that covers the whole sky is stratus, and thin, wispy streaks high up are cirrus.
If there are no clouds at all, write the word clear.
Then check the wind vane.
Its arrow points toward the direction the wind is coming from, and winds are named for the place they start.
So if the arrow points west, write west wind, even though the air is moving toward the east.
If the vane keeps swinging back and forth, watch it for one minute and write the direction it points to most often.
Last, write one sentence describing how the weather feels, such as cold and still or warm and breezy.
On Friday, look back over all five days and circle the warmest day and the coldest day.
Then write one sentence about how the clouds changed during the week.

passages.title: Pitching a Tent
sentences: The science club is spending one night at the campsite in Story Woods, and every group of three must pitch its own tent.
The camp leader gave each group these steps and asked everyone to read all of them before unpacking anything.
First, choose a flat spot that is a little higher than the ground around it, so rainwater will not collect under the tent.
Look up for dead branches, and do not set up the tent under them.
Clear away sticks, pinecones and stones, because even small ones will poke you through the floor all night.
Next, spread the ground sheet where the tent will go, and fold under any edges that stick out past the tent floor.
If the edges stick out, rain can land on the sheet and run underneath the tent.
Lay the tent on the ground sheet with its door facing away from the wind.
Slide the two long poles through the sleeves so they cross in an X.
Bend the poles and push their ends into the metal rings at the four corners, and the tent will rise into a dome.
Push a stake through each corner loop and into the ground at an angle, with the top of the stake leaning away from the tent.
Finally, check the weather report on the camp notice board.
If rain is possible tonight, put the rain fly over the tent and stake it out so it does not touch the tent walls.
If the night will be clear and dry, you can leave the fly off and see the stars through the mesh roof.
Before dark, make sure everyone in the group knows where the flashlight is.

passages.title: Planning a Hike to the Lookout
sentences: Sam and Leo are planning a hike to the lookout at the top of Lantern Peaks, and Sam is reading the trail map.
Two trails start at the parking lot: the Red Trail, which is 2 miles long, and the Blue Trail, which is 3 miles long.
Thin brown lines called contour lines curve across the map.
Each line joins points that are the same height above sea level, and on this map, each line is 50 feet higher than the one below it.
Where contour lines are close together, the ground is steep, and where they are far apart, the ground is gentle.
The Red Trail goes almost straight up across lines that are packed close together, so it is short but steep the whole way.
The Blue Trail winds back and forth across lines that are spread out, so it is longer but gentle.
The legend at the bottom of the map lists the trail rules.
Hikers should allow 30 minutes for each mile of gentle trail and 45 minutes for each mile of steep trail.
Everyone must be back at the parking lot by 6:00 PM, when the gate closes.
If the wind becomes strong, take the Blue Trail down, because the Red Trail's steep, open rocks are hard to cross in strong wind.
Sam plans to walk up the gentle Blue Trail and come back down the steep Red Trail, so they can see both.
He also plans a 30-minute rest at the lookout to eat lunch and look at the view.

passages.title: Kayak Lesson
sentences: Ana and Ben are taking a two-hour kayak lesson in the calm north corner of the harbor.
Before anyone touches a paddle, the instructor checks that every life jacket is zipped and buckled.
A life jacket fits well when it stays in place as the instructor lifts it by the shoulders, instead of sliding up past your ears.
To hold the paddle, grip the shaft with both hands a little wider apart than your shoulders, with your knuckles pointing up.
Make sure the scooped side of each blade faces you, because that side catches more water.
For a forward stroke, reach forward, dip one blade into the water near your feet, and pull it back to your hip.
Then lift that blade out and do the same on the other side.
To turn, use a sweep stroke.
Dip the blade near your feet and draw a wide half circle out to the side and back toward the back of the kayak.
A sweep on the right side turns the front of the kayak to the left, and a sweep on the left side turns it to the right.
To stop, dig the blade into the water beside your hip and push it forward, first on one side and then on the other.
Stay inside the area marked by the orange buoys, and keep at least two kayak lengths away from other boats.
If you hear one long whistle blast, stop paddling and look at the instructor.
If you hear three short blasts, paddle back to the dock right away.

items.prompt: Ben wants to turn the front of his kayak to the left. What should he do?
options: Do a sweep stroke on the left side
Do a sweep stroke on the right side
Dig the blade in beside his hip and push forward
Do forward strokes on both sides
items.hint: Find the sentence that tells which way each sweep turns the kayak. Read both halves carefully.
items.explain: He does a sweep stroke on the right side. The third paragraph says a sweep on the right side turns the front of the kayak to the left.

items.prompt: Ana hears three short whistle blasts. What should she do?
options: Stop paddling and look at the instructor
Paddle back to the dock right away
Paddle out to the orange buoys
Do a sweep stroke to turn around and wait
items.hint: Two sentences talk about the whistle. Find the one that matches three short blasts.
items.explain: She paddles back to the dock right away. The last sentence says three short blasts mean paddle back to the dock. One long blast means stop and look at the instructor.

items.prompt: The instructor lifts Ben's life jacket by the shoulders, and it slides up past his ears. What does this tell them?
options: The jacket fits well, so Ben can start paddling
The jacket does not fit well yet, so it needs to be fixed before Ben paddles
Ben is holding his paddle the wrong way
Ben should stay two kayak lengths away from other boats
items.hint: Find the sentence that says how to tell if a life jacket fits well. Compare it with what happens to Ben's jacket.
items.explain: The jacket does not fit well yet. The first paragraph says a jacket fits well when it stays in place as it is lifted, instead of sliding up past your ears.

steps.say: I need to put the steps in order. I look for order words like first, then and last.
This step starts with First. The banana and berries go in first.
This step starts with Then. The milk goes in next.
This step starts with Last. The lid goes on and they press START at the end.
So the order is fruit, then milk, then the lid and START.
